extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, attorneys, researchers and students interested in EPO case law on patentable subject-matter (especially computer-implemented inventions/software).
extracted.subtask_description: A compilation of Board of Appeal decisions and distilled principles for assessing whether subject-matter falls within the exclusions of Article 52(2) and (3) EPC (with emphasis on computer-related inventions). Useful for deciding if a claim is excluded as a non‑technical/mathematical/mental/administrative method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for inclusion in this decisions list
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision has been published on the Official Journal of the EPO (OJ), or will be published at the Official Journal, as indicated in the decision; and the decision explicitly mentions Article 52(2) and/or (3) EPC in the reasons, unless the mention is tangential or the case exclusively relates to procedural questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the page's meta‑criterion for which Board of Appeal decisions are collected here (cases with only tangential mentions or purely procedural issues are excluded from the main list).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural steps without technical means are excluded from patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim focuses solely on procedural steps involved in applying a coded distinctive mark to an object without indicating or presupposing technical means for carrying them out, a process of this kind is excluded from patentability by Article 52(2)(c) and (3) EPC. (T 51/84)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: purely administrative/organizational steps or manual procedures that do not require or specify technical means will be treated as excluded subject‑matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical methods underlying a claim do not automatically make it a non‑patentable mathematical method 'as such'
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that the idea or concept underlying the subject‑matter of a claim resides in a mathematical method does not necessarily mean that the claimed subject‑matter is a mathematical method 'as such'. (T 208/84)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim, considered as a whole, makes a technical contribution; mere reliance on a mathematical concept is not decisive if the claimed subject‑matter produces a technical effect or contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisive test: technical contribution of the claim as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: "Decisive is what technical contribution the invention as defined in the claim when considered as a whole makes to the known art." (T 208/84 cited on the page)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the claimed subject‑matter as a whole and identify any technical effect or technical solution to a technical problem; this is the central enquiry in borderline cases (e.g., computer‑implemented inventions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of technical considerations regarding particulars of the solution prevents exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A method was considered not excluded under Art. 52(2) and (3) EPC 'if technical considerations concerning particulars of the solution of the problem the invention solves are required in order to carry out that same invention.' (T 769/92)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If carrying out the invention requires technical choices/implementations (not just abstract steps), the subject‑matter is less likely to be excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: A method involving technical means is generally an invention under Article 52(1) EPC
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, a method involving technical means is an invention within the meaning of Article 52(1) EPC. (T 258/03; e.g., Auction Method/Hitachi)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere involvement of technical means (hardware, devices) ordinarily confers an 'invention' character, but further analysis (technical contribution, inventive step) remains necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'exclusions' (not inventions) from 'exceptions' (inventions denied protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain categories of subject‑matter are not regarded as inventions at all — these are sometimes called the exclusions (Article 52(2) and (3) EPC). In contrast, certain other categories, while being considered as inventions, are denied the protection of patents — these are sometimes called the exceptions (Article 53 EPC). (T 315/03)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conceptual distinction matters when classifying subject‑matter and applying the appropriate legal rule or remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive diagnostic decision phase is an intellectual exercise and not an invention; device may be an invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The deductive medical or veterinary decision phase (diagnosis for curative purposes) in itself is an intellectual exercise and, pursuant to Article 52(2) EPC, is not regarded as an invention, whereas the method carried out by a device capable of reaching diagnostic conclusions might well represent an invention. (G 1/04)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate purely mental/diagnostic reasoning (excluded) from technical apparatus or technical measurement and processing that implements diagnosis (may be patentable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject‑matter remains excluded even if it implies use of unspecified technical means
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject‑matter or activities that are excluded from patentability under Article 52(2) and (3) EPC remain so even where they imply the possibility of making use of unspecified technical means, such as an unspecified computer. (T 388/04)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely stating that an excluded method could be performed 'by a computer' or other unspecified technical means does not overcome the exclusion; the technical means must be meaningfully part of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural/abstract steps contribute to technical character only if they serve a technical purpose; simulations can be technical if essential to production
rubrics_metrics.description: A procedural step may contribute to the technical character of a claimed method only to the extent that it serves a technical purpose of the method. Simulation methods which form an essential part of the fabrication process and precede actual production, mostly as an intermediate step, cannot be denied a technical effect merely on the grounds that they do not yet incorporate the physical end product. (T 1227/05 / Schaltkreissimulation I / Infineon Technologies)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the step or simulation serves a concrete technical purpose in a technical process (e.g., fabrication), not merely abstract modelling; being essential to a technical workflow supports technical character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty objections and Article 52(2)/(3) objections are distinct and may coexist
rubrics_metrics.description: Concurrent novelty objections and objections under Article 52(2) and (3) EPC could exist, but they are distinct objections. (G 2/88 noted by the page)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a claim, treat novelty and excluded‑subject‑matter enquiries separately; a finding on one does not automatically resolve the other.
